text.Google Shape;185;p28: A voice and a pulse monitor for patients who cannot speak or move

slides.notes: Imagine being fully awake, in pain, and unable to say a single word. Many Tunisian patients live this every day. We built 3ayni, my eyes, to give them a voice.

After a stroke, with ALS, or on a breathing tube, many patients understand everything but cannot speak or move. Families guess from blinks, eye-gaze devices cost thousands of dinars, and nobody hears their silent distress.

text.Google Shape;433;p42: Rules combine the words and the heart rate
text.Google Shape;434;p42: The caregiver's phone gets the message and alert

slides.notes: Everything runs in the browser on the bedside laptop. A face model tracks the eyes, and an eight-second calibration learns this patient's gaze. Each heartbeat slightly changes skin colour, which gives the heart rate. Clear rules combine words and body, and the phone gets the result.

Live demo, about ninety seconds. A jury member follows five dots to calibrate, then says I want to drink with their eyes, and the laptop speaks it. Their heart rate appears on screen and on the phone. We start the stress scenario, answer pain, and the phone shows an urgent alert. One tap, and the patient sees help is coming.

We used AI only where rules cannot work: tracking the eyes and learning each patient's gaze. The pulse uses a published signal method with no training data, suggestions use a small offline model, and alerts are simple rules a nurse can trust.

Suggestions cut the effort of a message by 37 percent, measured on 2,000 simulated conversations the model never saw. On test signals the heart rate stays within 3 beats, even under flickering light, and all 63 automated tests pass. Real-world accuracy against a pulse oximeter comes next.

slides.notes: Video never leaves the laptop. A phone connects only with the code shown at the bedside. A weak signal shows a dash, never a guess. And because camera heart rate can be less accurate on darker skin, our logger measures that against a reference device.
